name: THE GREEN A LITTLE BEAN OF ME BURGER

recipe.history:
The green bean — known botanically as Phaseolus vulgaris and variously called haricot vert, string bean, snap bean, or French bean depending on where in the world you encounter it — was first cultivated in the highlands of Peru and Mexico thousands of years before European contact, forming part of the 'Three Sisters' agricultural tradition alongside corn and squash that sustained Mesoamerican civilizations. Spanish and Portuguese explorers carried the bean back to Europe in the 16th century, where it spread rapidly through the Mediterranean and eventually northward. In France, the bean was cultivated into increasingly slender, tender varieties — the haricot vert, 'green bean' in French — that prioritized delicacy over yield, and French cuisine elevated this humble legume into an art form. The French method of quickly blanching and then sautéing haricot verts in butter with shallots and garlic became one of the foundational side dishes of classical cuisine, and the bean's combination of verdant freshness, slight grassiness, and crisp-tender texture made it one of the most versatile vegetables in any kitchen.

Blistered haricot verts — cooked in a screaming-hot pan with a bare minimum of oil until the pods char in spots, wrinkle, and develop a concentrated, almost nutty sweetness — became a fashionable restaurant preparation in the 2010s, driven by the broader American embrace of high-heat vegetable cookery that produced similar revelations with broccoli, Brussels sprouts, and cauliflower. When a blister-cooked green bean hits a burger, it adds something no traditional burger topping provides: a charred, slightly sweet, grassy crunch that cuts through beef fat with botanical freshness. The bean aioli — made from puréed cooked white beans with lemon, garlic, and olive oil — extends the legume theme as a creamy, subtle spread that adds protein and earthiness without overwhelming the other flavors.

I started blistering vegetables at a high temperature because I am constitutionally impatient and a properly blistered vegetable cooks in under five minutes. The first time I put blistered haricots verts on a burger it was because I had nothing else in the fridge that seemed appropriate and a handful of the beans on the counter that were one day away from losing their snap. I threw them in a dry cast iron pan on high heat, tossed them for three or four minutes until they blistered and charred in spots, hit them with a little flaky salt and olive oil, and piled them on a medium rare patty spread with bean aioli. The result was so good that I deliberately made the same grocery situation recur several times until I had the recipe refined to my satisfaction.

Medium rare is the correct temperature for this burger — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, 54 to 57 Celsius — and the combination of blistered green beans and bean aioli makes the argument especially compelling. Both the beans and the aioli are vegetable-forward flavors: fresh, clean, slightly earthy, and relatively delicate. They need a beef patty that is itself fully expressive — juicy, pink, mineral, richly beefy — not a well-done puck that retreats behind the toppings. Medium rare beef meets the haricots verts and the bean aioli as an equal third party in the flavor conversation. All three are present; all three contribute. That is the standard to cook to.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
1 can (400g) white cannellini beans, drained and rinsed
instructions: 1. Make the white bean aioli: Combine drained cannellini beans, garlic, olive oil, lemon juice, Dijon mustard, white pepper, and salt in a food processor. Blend until very smooth, adding water one tablespoon at a time to reach a thick, spreadable consistency. Taste and adjust lemon and salt. Transfer to a bowl and refrigerate until needed.

2. Make the buns: Combine warm milk, yeast, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, egg, and butter. Knead with dough hook on medium for 8 minutes until smooth. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 equal portions, shape into smooth balls, and place on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Cover and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash, sprinkle with sesame seeds, and bake 16 to 18 minutes until golden. Cool on a wire rack.

3. Blister the haricots verts: Heat a large cast iron skillet over very high heat until it just begins to smoke. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Add the green beans in a single layer — work in batches if needed to avoid steaming. Cook undisturbed for 2 minutes. Toss and cook another 2 minutes until the beans are blistered, charred in spots, and tender-crisp. Add the sliced garlic for the last 30 seconds, tossing constantly. Transfer to a bowl and immediately drizzle with olive oil, sprinkle flaky sea salt and red pepper flakes, and squeeze lemon juice over the top. Set aside.

4. Shape the patties: Season ground beef with salt, black pepper, and garlic powder. Divide into 4 equal portions and shape into patties 3/4 inch thick and slightly wider than the buns. Press a dimple into the center of each.
5. Wipe the skillet briefly and return to high heat. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties undisturbed for 3 minutes to develop a deep crust.

6. Flip patties and lay a slice of Gruyère on each. Cook 2 to 3 more minutes, checking temperature with an instant-read thermometer. Remove patties at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Tent with foil and rest 3 to 4 minutes.
7. Toast buns cut-side down in residual skillet fat for 60 to 90 seconds until golden.

8. Assemble: Spread white bean aioli generously on both cut sides of the bun. Place butter lettuce on the bottom bun, then the patty with melted Gruyère. Pile a generous mound of blistered haricots verts on top of the patty. Squeeze a little fresh lemon juice over the beans before closing the bun. Serve immediately.
